106.title: When prayer feels empty
106.hook: you pray and feel nothing; the Psalms have a name and a picture for it
106.howItsDone: Many Christians go through dry seasons in prayer. Priests, pastors and spiritual directors commonly suggest keeping prayer short and honest, leaning on set prayers like the Psalms, and talking it over with someone they trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lament: Psalm 13's how long. Your line was complaint is a prayer too. Did the thing you wrote shift overnight? Today, the quieter problem: not anger, just nothing. Day one hundred six.

Ten seconds in, the mind has already wandered off: the email, the thing someone said at lunch. You bring it back. You say the words. And it feels like talking into a phone after the call has quietly dropped. Nothing on the other end. Not anger. Not exactly doubt. Just nothing. On Christian forums people confess this again and again: prayer feels empty, even fake, and they wonder what's wrong with them. Here's the surprise. The Bible's own prayer book has a picture for exactly this, and it's spoken to God, not about him. Today's word is the old name for it.
screen: `TALKING INTO A DROPPED CALL.` → `NOT ANGER. JUST NOTHING.` → `THE BIBLE HAS A PICTURE FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Dryness. Christian writers have used that word for centuries for prayer that feels like nothing. The picture comes from the Psalms. One prays, in the King James Bible: "my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is." Another, from someone far from the temple, says: "My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God," while people keep asking, "Where is thy God?" So the feeling isn't a modern failure. It sits in the Bible's prayer book, prayed by people who kept praying. Catholic and Orthodox spiritual writers teach that dryness comes and goes; later on this path you'll meet John of the Cross and his dark night. Many evangelical pastors call it a dry season. C. S. Lewis wrote a book of letters from a senior devil to a junior one, and the devil admits what worries him most: a person who feels nothing, still intends to do God's will, and keeps going. So what do people do in a dry stretch? Keep it small: one honest sentence. Borrow words, a psalm or the Lord's Prayer, when your own run out. Tell someone: a pastor, a priest, a friend who prays. And look at the rest of life, because sleep, grief and stress all dry the ground. One more thing, said plainly. If the flatness isn't only in prayer, if food, friends and the things you love have gone gray too, that can be depression. It's an illness, not a failure of faith, and seeing a doctor or a counselor isn't a lack of faith either. If you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `A DRY AND THIRSTY LAND.` · `WHERE IS THY GOD?` · `STILL INTENDING, STILL GOING.` · `WHEN IT'S MORE THAN PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit dry. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to feel anything. That's the whole point today. If you pray, say one honest sentence, maybe the psalm's own: my soul thirsteth. Or simply: I don't feel you, and I'm here anyway. Then stay, and let nothing happen. If you don't pray, just sit, and notice that showing up still counts when it's quiet. The bell holds the time.
Dryness. The old Christian name for prayer that feels like nothing, pictured in the Psalms as a dry and thirsty land. Today's word.
Your line: a dry prayer still counts. If prayer feels empty today, one honest sentence is enough. Day one hundred six.

107.title: The daily office
107.hook: Anglicans pray the Book of Common Prayer morning and evening, with short set prayers called collects
107.howItsDone: Many Anglicans and Episcopalians pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer, at home or in church, ending with set collects; cathedrals often sing Evensong daily, and Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep their own daily hours of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dryness, prayer in a dry and thirsty land, and your line: a dry prayer still counts. Did one honest sentence do? Today, prayers with a timetable, for when your own words run dry. Day one hundred seven.

Five thirty on a weekday in an English cathedral. Outside, traffic and buses. Inside, a choir in robes, a dozen people in the old wooden seats, and the same service that has been sung there, in some form, for centuries. It's called Evensong. It goes back to 1549, when Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, took the church's daily prayers, which were in Latin and spread across many services through the day, shaped for monks, and put them into English, in two: one for morning, one for evening. He called his book the Book of Common Prayer. Common, as in shared. Anyone could pray it, at home or in church. And tucked into both services are tiny prayers, a single sentence each. Today's word is their name.

A collect. Say it with the stress at the front: COLL-ect. It's a short set prayer with a shape. It speaks to God, often recalls something about God, asks for one thing, and closes through Christ. One breath, one request. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from. One old idea is that it collects the silent prayers of everyone present into one sentence. The whole rhythm is called the daily office, from the Latin for duty or service. The habit is older than the church: the Psalms speak of praying "Evening, and morning, and at noon," and Daniel prayed three times a day. Near the end of Evening Prayer comes the collect for aid against all perils. Cranmer translated it from an old Latin night prayer. In the 1662 Book of Common Prayer: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night; for the love of thy only Son, our Saviour, Jesus Christ. Amen." Picture the world it was written for. No streetlights. Night meant real danger: fire, illness, thieves, the dark itself. People said it before bed, and some still do. Anglicans and Episcopalians pray it, and some Methodists too. Catholics keep their own daily office, the Liturgy of the Hours, and the Orthodox pray Vespers at evening and Matins at morning. Different books, the same idea: time itself, marked with prayer, morning and evening, like a heartbeat.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the evening collect, or simply hear it. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say it slowly, out loud or under your breath: Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night. If you don't pray, just let the words pass through you, and notice which phrase stays. Then think of one darkness, yours or someone else's, that could use some light tonight. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LIGHTEN OUR DARKNESS, WE BESEECH THEE, O LORD.`

108.title: In your own words
108.hook: many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray freely and aloud, like talking to a friend
108.howItsDone: Many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians pray aloud in their own words, alone or in small groups, taking turns; many Christians mix this kind of free prayer with set prayers like the Lord's Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the collect, a prayer of one sentence, and your line: lighten our darkness. Did you say it when the last light went out? Yesterday's words were written in 1549. Today's are made up on the spot. Day one hundred eight.

A Wednesday night in a small church, or a living room. Ten people in a circle. No book. Somebody starts: Lord, thank you for this week. We just bring you Maria's mom. You know what she needs. Then someone else picks it up, and someone else. Plain words, half sentences, a laugh, a long pause. It sounds less like a service and more like a conversation with someone who's in the room. For many evangelical and Pentecostal Christians, this is what prayer mostly is. And they'd point to a line in Exodus about Moses: "the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend." Today closes our twelve days on ways to pray, with the simplest one.
screen: `A CIRCLE, NO BOOK.` → `PLAIN WORDS, HALF SENTENCES.` → `AS A MAN SPEAKETH UNTO HIS FRIEND.`

segments.voice: In your own words. Christians call it free prayer, or extemporaneous prayer: no script, just speaking. It grew strong among the Puritans, then Baptists and Methodists, and later Pentecostals, who wanted prayer to come from the heart as well as the book. They find it all through the Bible. Hannah, longing for a child, prays in the temple with her lips moving and no sound, and the priest thinks she's drunk. She tells him she has "poured out my soul before the LORD." A psalm says it plainly: "ye people, pour out your heart before him." All of it. The rent, the kid, the test. And Hebrews says, "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace." The Greek word behind boldly is parresia: speaking freely, saying everything, holding nothing back. What if you don't know what to say? Paul has an answer for that: the Spirit helps, he says, praying in us with groans that words can't carry. Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians also pray in tongues, which they understand as a gift of the Spirit; other Christians read those passages differently. Many Christians use both kinds of prayer: set words when their own run out, their own words when the set ones feel far away. Looking back on these twelve days, you've met them all: a pattern, a name, a psalm, a slow reading, a look back, an arrow, a list of names, a complaint, a dry spell, a collect. And now, just talk.
screen: `FREE PRAYER: NO SCRIPT.` · `HANNAH POURED OUT HER SOUL.` · `POUR OUT YOUR HEART, BOLDLY.` · `SET WORDS AND YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk out loud for one minute. It may feel strange. That's fine. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, talk to God the way you'd talk to a friend who already knows everything: what happened today, what you're worried about, what you're glad about. Plain words. Half sentences are fine. If you don't pray, say out loud what's on your mind, and what you're grateful for. Out loud matters: it slows you down and makes it real. When the minute's done, stop, and listen to the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Parresia, the Greek word for boldness: speaking freely to God without holding anything back, the way you'd talk to a friend.

Your line: just talk. Today, once, in the car or on a walk, say something out loud to God, or to the quiet, in your own plain words. Tomorrow, a new stretch: the circle of the year. Day one hundred eight.

109.title: Time as a circle
109.hook: many churches walk the life of Christ every year, with colors and seasons
109.howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and many Methodist and Presbyterian churches follow the liturgical year, changing colors, readings and prayers with each season; many other churches celebrate mainly Christmas and Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in your own words, parresia, and your line: just talk. Did you say something out loud, in the car or on a walk? That closed twelve days of ways to pray. Now, twelve days on the circle of the year. Day one hundred nine.

Sit in the same church once a month for a year and watch the cloth on the altar. Late November, it turns purple, or in some churches deep blue. At Christmas, white and gold. Then back to green for a while. Toward spring, purple again, for weeks. At Easter, white, bursting with lilies. One Sunday in late spring, everything is suddenly red. Then green, for months and months, all through the summer and fall. Nobody announces it. It's just there, like leaves changing on a tree outside the window. Those colors are a clock. A calendar you can see from the back row. Today's word is the name of the whole circle.
screen: `PURPLE, WHITE, GREEN, RED.` → `NOBODY ANNOUNCES IT.` → `A CLOCK FROM THE BACK ROW.`

segments.voice: The liturgical year. Liturgy comes from the Greek leitourgia, a public work or service, often explained as the work of the people. The liturgical year is the church's calendar, and it doesn't count money or school terms. It walks through the life of Jesus, every single year. It begins, in the Western churches, with Advent: four weeks of waiting in the dark before Christmas. Then Christmas itself, the birth. Then Epiphany, God shown to the world. Then Lent, forty days in the desert. Then Holy Week, the cross, and Easter, the empty tomb. Then Pentecost, the Spirit, fifty days later. And then the long green stretch the church calls ordinary time. Easter moves every year, because it follows the moon; Christmas stays put. The Orthodox year starts in a different place, on the first of September, and runs its own rhythm of feasts and fasts. The book of Ecclesiastes says: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Here's the idea underneath. Daily life runs on time as a line: deadlines, birthdays, one year after another. The church year makes time a circle too. You come back to the same stories every year, and you're a different person each time you meet them. The birth sounds different the year you have a baby. The cross sounds different the year you lose someone. Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans keep the full year, as do many Methodists and Presbyterians; many Baptist, evangelical and Pentecostal churches mark mainly Christmas and Easter. For those who keep it, the circle makes the calendar itself holy.
screen: `LEITOURGIA: A PUBLIC SERVICE.` · `A YEAR THROUGH THE LIFE OF JESUS.` · `A TIME TO EVERY PURPOSE.` · `TIME AS A LINE, AND A CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find yourself on the circle. Settle, and breathe. Picture the seasons going round: waiting, birth, light, desert, cross, empty tomb, fire, and then the long green ordinary. Don't worry about the calendar date right now. Ask which season your own life feels like this month. Waiting for something? In a desert? Somewhere ordinary and green? If you pray, you can bring that season to God as it is. If you don't, just name it, and sit with it. Later today, look up where the church calendar actually is. The bell holds the time.
Liturgical year. The church's calendar of seasons and colors, walking through the life of Christ every year. Today's word.
Your line: time can be holy. Today, look up the season and color of the church calendar right now, and notice one thing in your week that matches it. Day one hundred nine.

110.title: Advent: waiting
110.hook: four weeks of candles and longing before Christmas
110.howItsDone: Many Christians keep Advent with a wreath of four candles lit one more each Sunday, with daily readings and quieter, expectant hymns; Orthodox Christians keep a forty-day Nativity fast before Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the liturgical year, and your line: time can be holy. Did you find where the church calendar is right now? Today, the place the circle begins. Day one hundred ten.

Think about the last time you really waited for something. A baby due any day. Test results. A plane landing with someone you love on it. That strange mix: you can't make it come faster, and you can't stop looking at the door. Now picture a round wreath of evergreen on a kitchen table in December, with four candles in it. On the first Sunday, one candle is lit. The next week, two. Then three. Then four. Outside, the nights keep getting longer. Inside, the light slowly grows. The shops have been playing Christmas songs since early November, but in many churches the songs are still about the dark, and about longing. Today's word is the name of that waiting.
screen: `WAITING AT THE DOOR.` → `FOUR CANDLES, ONE A WEEK.` → `THE LIGHT SLOWLY GROWS.`

segments.voice: Advent. From the Latin adventus, a coming, an arrival. It's the four Sundays before Christmas, and in Western churches it's where the church year begins. Here's what surprises people: Advent looks two ways at once. Back, to the first coming, the birth in Bethlehem, and all the centuries of hoping before it. And forward, to what Christians call the second coming, when they believe Christ will return and set the world right. So the readings are full of prophets. Isaiah: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light." John the Baptist in the desert, telling everyone to get ready. The mood is purple: hope, but with an ache in it. Many churches sing the old hymn O Come, O Come, Emmanuel, which sounds more like a plea than a party. The wreath is younger than people think. It's usually traced to a Lutheran pastor in nineteenth-century Germany who made a wheel of candles to help the children in his care count down the days. Many wreaths now have three purple candles and one pink, for the third Sunday, when the mood turns toward joy; some add a white one in the middle for Christmas Day. Orthodox Christians keep a longer season before Christmas, a forty-day fast. And the whole thing ends with the Bible's own last prayer, in Revelation: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Advent says waiting isn't wasted time. For Christians it's a kind of prayer: keeping the door open, and the light on.
screen: `ADVENTUS: A COMING.` · `BACK TO BETHLEHEM, FORWARD TO THE END.` · `A WREATH, ONE CANDLE A WEEK.` · then, large: `EVEN SO, COME, LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle and wait. If you have one, and it's safe, light it now. If not, turn on one small lamp, or just picture a flame. Settle, and breathe. Don't do anything. Don't reach for your phone. Just wait, and watch the light. Notice how hard it is to wait for nothing in particular. If you pray, you can say the old line, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus," once, and then wait some more. If you don't, let yourself notice what you're longing for. The bell holds the time.
Advent. From the Latin for coming. Four weeks of waiting and longing before Christmas, where the church year begins. Today's word.
Your line: come, lord. Today, when you have to wait, in a line, on hold, at a red light, don't fill it. Let it be Advent for thirty seconds. Day one hundred ten.

111.title: Christmas: twelve days
111.hook: Christmas is a season, not a day, running to 6 January
111.howItsDone: Many Christians go to church on Christmas Eve or Christmas Day and keep celebrating through the twelve days to Epiphany; many Orthodox Christians celebrate on January 7, following the Julian calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Advent, four weeks of waiting, and your line: come, lord. Did you let a red light or a line be Advent for thirty seconds? Today, the waiting ends. Day one hundred eleven.

December twenty-sixth. Wrapping paper in bags by the door. Radio stations quietly switching back to regular music. By New Year's, trees are lying on the curb, a little brown, a few strands of tinsel still caught in the branches. Christmas: done. Here's the surprise. For many churches, on December twenty-sixth, Christmas has barely started. There's the old song about a partridge in a pear tree, with gifts piling up day after day. That song is counting something real. Christmas, in the church's calendar, isn't a day. It's a season: twelve days long, running up to the sixth of January. Today's word is the season, and the thing it celebrates.
screen: `DECEMBER 26: TREES ON THE CURB.` → `A PARTRIDGE IN A PEAR TREE.` → `A SEASON, NOT A DAY.`

segments.voice: Christmas. Old English, Christ's Mass: the feast of Christ. It celebrates what Christians call the incarnation, God becoming a human being. John's Gospel says it this way: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." And Matthew gives the name the prophet promised: "Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." That's the heart of it. Not God far off, watching. God with us, as a baby who needs feeding. Then the twelve days. They run from Christmas Day to the eve of the sixth of January, which is Epiphany, the day the wise men arrive. And the days in between aren't only cozy. In Western churches, the day after Christmas remembers Stephen, whom tradition calls the first Christian martyr. A few days later, the children Herod killed in Bethlehem. The season holds joy and grief in the same hands, like many families at the holidays. Now, a question people ask: was Jesus really born on December twenty-fifth? The Gospels never say. They give no date at all. By the fourth century, Christians in Rome kept the feast on that day, and scholars still debate why. And many Orthodox Christians, who follow the older Julian calendar, celebrate Christmas on what the rest of the world calls January seventh. Same feast, different calendar. Underneath, the twelve days make one point. If God with us is true, Christians say, it's too big for one day. You don't unwrap it in an afternoon. You keep celebrating.
screen: `CHRIST'S MASS: THE FEAST OF CHRIST.` · `EMMANUEL, GOD WITH US.` · `TWELVE DAYS, JOY AND GRIEF.` · `THE GOSPELS GIVE NO DATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go back to something good. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing from the last few weeks that you moved past too quickly. A kind word. A meal. A win. A laugh with someone. Go back to it now. Let yourself feel it again, slowly, the way you'd look at a gift a second time. If you pray, you can give thanks for it, and for God with us. If you don't, just stay with the gladness. Then decide one small way to keep celebrating it this week. The bell holds the time.
Christmas. Christ's Mass: the feast of God with us, and in the church's calendar, a season of twelve days. Today's word.
Your line: god with us. Today, keep celebrating one good thing after its day is over. Tell someone about it again. Day one hundred eleven.

112.title: Epiphany: the light spreads
112.hook: the magi, the baptism, the wedding at Cana: God shown to the world
112.howItsDone: Western churches celebrate Epiphany on January 6 with the story of the magi, and some families bless their doors with chalk; Orthodox churches keep Theophany, remembering Christ's baptism with the blessing of the waters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve days of Christmas, and your line: god with us. Did you keep celebrating something? This week: an icon, a collect, your own words, the circle of the year, Advent's waiting, Christmas. Today the twelve days end. Day one hundred twelve.

Strangers arrive in a small town. They've come a long way, from somewhere east. Matthew calls them wise men; they read the sky, and they say a star has led them here. In the King James words: "for we have seen his star in the east, and are come to worship him." They find a house in Bethlehem, a young mother and a child. And these foreigners kneel on the floor and open their treasures: gold, frankincense and myrrh. In Matthew's Gospel, the ones who come to worship the child are outsiders from far away. Today's word is the feast that tells their story, and then keeps going.

segments.voice: Epiphany. From the Greek epiphaneia: an appearing, a showing. It falls on the sixth of January, the day after the twelve days end. And it's really about one idea, told in three stories. God shown to the world. First, the magi: the light reaching people from outside, from far away. Western churches put the wise men at the center of the day. Second, the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan, when a voice from heaven calls him beloved. Orthodox churches call the feast Theophany, God shown, and center it there. Priests bless the waters, and in some places they throw a cross into a cold river or the sea, and swimmers dive in after it. Third, a wedding at Cana, where Jesus turns water into wine. John writes: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee, and manifested forth his glory." Three stories. One showing. And the thread through all of it is who gets to see. The prophet Isaiah had said, "And the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising." Gentiles means the nations, everyone who wasn't Jewish. So Epiphany is the season when Christians say the light spreads outward, to everybody. People keep it in their own ways. In Spain and parts of Latin America, Three Kings Day is when children get their presents. Some families write the year and the letters C, M and B above their front door in chalk, a blessing for the house. And in everyday English, an epiphany is a sudden moment when something becomes clear. That everyday sense borrows its name from this feast.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for what's being shown. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day. Was there a moment when something became clear? A person you saw differently. A problem that suddenly made sense. Something beautiful you almost walked past. It can be small. Let it come back to you, and look at it again. If you pray, you can give thanks for what was shown. If you don't, just notice that seeing happened. Then stay open for the rest of the time. The bell holds the time.
Epiphany. From the Greek for a showing. The feast on January 6, when Christians remember God shown to the whole world. Today's word.
Your line: the light is for everyone. Today, notice one person you'd usually count as an outsider, and look for what they might be showing you. Sixteen weeks on the path. Day one hundred twelve.
